body: Pa. advocates rally for vote on bill that would tax big tech ad platforms. A rally at the state Capitol in favor of taxing wealthy individuals and large tech companies, June 1, 2026.Zack Hoopes. Tax reform advocates gathered in the Capitol on Monday to promote several proposals to make the wealthiest corporations and individuals in the state pay a greater share, and to celebrate the fact that one proposal is expected to finally get a vote. But a bill to establish a tax on online advertising platforms - one of the measures supported by those who rallied Monday - is likely to at least get a committee vote this week. Remarks by lawmakers and activists focused on three proposals: implementing combined reporting to prevent corporations from sheltering profits with out-of-state subsidiaries; charging a higher personal income tax rate on capital gains, royalties, and other sources of income disproportionately received by the wealthy; and expanding the gross receipts tax to include digital advertising shown to users in the commonwealth.

# New legislation to tax Big Tech’s digital advertising considered by PA House committee. **HARRISBURG, April 29 -**The PA House Finance Committee today considered H.B. 1678, new legislation that would tax revenue derived from digital advertising platforms. The bill, known as the Digital Ads Tax, was introduced by state Reps. House Bill 1678 would extend the existing gross receipts tax -- a 5% tax already paid by telecommunications and other industries -- to revenue from digital advertising platforms, which sell ad space on websites and apps. “I appreciate Chair Fiedler for introducing this legislation and thank the members of the committee for their thoughtful discussion on the proposal today,” said state Rep. Steve Samuelson, chair of the House Finance Committee. # Pa. Democrats think a tax on big tech companies could help the state’s deficit. ## The proposal would implement a 5% gross receipts tax on digital advertising platforms. A proposal in the state House would place a tax on companies that serve digital advertisements to Pennsylvanians through their phones and computers. It would do this by imposing a 5% gross receipts tax on revenue from digital advertising services in Pennsylvania. But its critics say it could cost businesses across the commonwealth that advertise on platforms like Google and Facebook, which could raise prices in the state to compensate. Another backer who testified Wednesday, Gabriela Noa Betancourt, the senior director of research at Action Center on Race and the Economy, said the measure is not intended to cost companies that advertise on platforms like Facebook and Google, but to extract a tax from the tech companies themselves, which make products used by millions of Pennsylvanians.
